column12: SYNTHETIC For most of high school I was the kid who joined everything and finished nothing, which is a harder habit to break than it sounds. What changed is not my ambition but my patience with the parts of a project that are slow and unglamorous. I stopped optimizing for looking competent and started optimizing for learning fast, and the difference showed up within a semester. The biggest shift has been learning to ask for help before I have exhausted every other option, which used to feel like losing. I still have the restlessness, but it points somewhere now.
column13: SYNTHETIC A professor told me my analysis was confident and unsupported, and she was right on both counts. I went back through what I had assumed and found that I had never once asked a potential user a question I did not already know the answer to. It took me longer than it should have to separate the disappointment from the information inside it. I treat early rejection as cheap information rather than a verdict, which has made me much faster.
column14: SYNTHETIC I built a free tool that helps transfer students figure out which of their credits actually count. I tracked one number weekly and killed the features that did not move it. The first step was talking to eleven people who had the problem, before I wrote a single line of anything. The thing I am proudest of is that it outlasted my involvement.
column15: SYNTHETIC Student organizations rebuild the same operational infrastructure every year because nothing is handed down. The first small experiment would be a one-week manual version: a spreadsheet and a form, no code at all. I would test whether people would use it at all by faking the backend and doing the work by hand for ten users. If nobody uses the manual version, the automated version was never the answer.
column16: SYNTHETIC What draws me is that Spark SC builds things for the campus rather than pitching things at it. I have run events end to end and I know how much of the work happens after the excitement wears off. I would bring operational follow-through, which is the least glamorous and most missing skill in student organizations. I am less interested in being in the room than in making the room work.
column17: SYNTHETIC I used to believe that the best idea wins, and that execution was a detail people used as an excuse. A friend showed me their retention data, and it turned out that useful and used are unrelated properties. The evidence was boring and undeniable: every project I did alone stalled at exactly the point where it needed someone else to care. What changed my mind was watching a worse idea, executed relentlessly, beat mine over a single semester. I try to write down what would change my mind before I get attached to being right.

column13: SYNTHETIC I was cut from a startup accelerator in the first round of interviews and spent a week convinced the feedback was wrong. What actually stung was that the feedback was specific, which meant I could not dismiss it as a matter of taste. I rebuilt the whole thing around the one piece of feedback I had been most defensive about. That experience is why I no longer wait until something is polished to show it to someone.
column14: SYNTHETIC I built a free tool that helps transfer students figure out which of their credits actually count. I recruited two friends by giving them ownership of a piece rather than tasks, and they are still involved. I set a hard deadline of four weeks for something usable, and shipped something embarrassing on time instead of something good late. It taught me that the constraint is almost never the idea.

A friend showed me their retention data, and it turned out that useful and used are unrelated properties. I try to write down what would change my mind before I get attached to being right.

column12: SYNTHETIC Before USC I spent two years working weekends at my family's restaurant, and I did not think of that as experience until recently. I found a group of people who take their work seriously without taking themselves seriously, and I started doing the same. I stopped optimizing for looking competent and started optimizing for learning fast, and the difference showed up within a semester. I still have the restlessness, but it points somewhere now.
column13: SYNTHETIC I was cut from a startup accelerator in the first round of interviews and spent a week convinced the feedback was wrong. I went back through what I had assumed and found that I had never once asked a potential user a question I did not already know the answer to. What actually stung was that the feedback was specific, which meant I could not dismiss it as a matter of taste. It took me longer than it should have to separate the disappointment from the information inside it. Now I go looking for the version of the feedback I would least like to hear, because that is usually the useful one.
column14: SYNTHETIC I started a tutoring program at my old high school and ran it for two years. The first step was talking to eleven people who had the problem, before I wrote a single line of anything. I recruited two friends by giving them ownership of a piece rather than tasks, and they are still involved. The thing I am proudest of is that it outlasted my involvement.
column15: SYNTHETIC Club recruitment at USC is opaque: applicants cannot tell what any organization actually wants until after they are rejected. I would start by asking twenty students to describe the problem in their own words before proposing anything. The first small experiment would be a one-week manual version: a spreadsheet and a form, no code at all. I would test whether people would use it at all by faking the backend and doing the work by hand for ten users. If nobody uses the manual version, the automated version was never the answer.
